sources.title: Sennacherib and Jerusalem
sources.author: Ira Spar · The Metropolitan Museum of Art
sources.summary: The museum looks at old writings, wall pictures, and the Bible. These sources tell about the war in 701 BCE. Judah lost many towns, but Jerusalem lived.
sources.limitations: The museum joins several sources. We still do not know why Assyria left.

sources.studyText: Assyrian writings and wall pictures tell about Judah’s losses. The Bible tells how Jerusalem lived. Each source has a different goal. We still do not know why Assyria left.

sources.title: Isaiah 36–39: rethinking priority and historical reliability
sources.author: Joel E. Anderson and Pieter M. Venter · HTS 65(1)
sources.summary: The writers compare Isaiah with the same story in Kings. They think Isaiah’s form came first. They study words that repeat and where the story was placed.
sources.limitations: Other experts do not agree. Kings may have come first. Both books may also use an older source.
sources.license: Linked reading; original study guide summary, no article reproduction
sources.studyText: Joel E. Anderson and Pieter M. Venter argue that Isaiah 36–39 forms a coherent account and may have been written before the parallel account in Kings. They connect its purpose with debate after Sennacherib’s invasion. These are scholarly arguments, not settled dates or proof of every reported event.

sources.title: My claim about Isaiah 53 is “demonstrably false”?
sources.author: Dan McClellan
sources.summary: McClellan says the servant is Israel. He links the servant’s pain with exile. He says an old Aramaic Bible does not show a dying Messiah before the time of Jesus. The books he cites do not rule out every earlier idea.
sources.limitations: This video is about Isaiah 49 and 53. It gives McClellan’s view of history. It is not Church teaching. Experts still debate who the servant is. Missing proof does not prove that an idea never existed.
sources.reviewed: English auto-captions reviewed. Publication titles checked against publisher or university records.

sources.title: What is Deutero-Isaiah?
sources.author: Dan McClellan
sources.summary: Second Isaiah is a name for Isaiah 40–55. McClellan thinks these chapters came from a later time. Chapter 39 warns of exile. Chapter 40 speaks as if exile has begun. He also finds new words and a new style.
sources.limitations: This is one expert view. The video does not review all the proof. A new chapter does not prove that a new person wrote it. The words we checked did not name another study.
sources.reviewed: English auto-captions and video date reviewed.

sources.title: Does the Great Isaiah Scroll prove the Bible hasn’t changed?
sources.author: Dan McClellan
sources.summary: McClellan compares two old Hebrew copies of Isaiah 53. Many changes are only spelling. Some changes affect the words or their meaning. One copy has the word “light” in verse 11. The text was kept well, but it did change.
sources.limitations: We did not check the video’s number totals. One chapter cannot show how much the whole Bible changed. The date of a copy is not the date when the book was first written.
sources.reviewed: English auto-captions reviewed. The cited edition’s identity and scope were checked with its publisher.
sources.license: Linked resource; original study guide summary. Video, transcript, and publication text are not reproduced.

sources.title: What’s going on with “line upon line” in Isaiah 28:10?

sources.title: The Glory of Israel: The Theology and Provenience of the Isaiah Targum
sources.author: Bruce D. Chilton
sources.summary: Studies how the Isaiah Targum developed across the first through fourth centuries CE. A Targum is an Aramaic translation that also interprets the text. McClellan cites Chilton at 3:31 when discussing stages of interpretation around 70–135 CE. The useful distinction is between a text’s surviving form and earlier traditions within it.
sources.limitations: Publisher description and the excerpt read in the video were reviewed, not the complete book. The proposed dates describe layers of interpretation. They do not date every sentence. The linked edition’s date differs from the 1982 original cited in the video.
sources.reviewed: Publisher record checked. Video excerpt supplies the specific dating discussion.

sources.title: The Suffering Servant between the Testaments
sources.author: S. H. T. Page
sources.summary: Examines whether a messianic interpretation of the suffering servant existed before Christianity. In the conclusion read at 5:10–6:55, Page rejects claims of uniform interpretation. He also rejects ruling out earlier possibilities. He considers a developed expectation of a Messiah who atones through suffering unlikely, while allowing preparatory ideas. This qualification matters when assessing McClellan’s stronger opening wording.
sources.limitations: Cambridge’s record, extract, and references were accessible. The conclusion was reviewed through McClellan’s reading, not a complete independent reading of the article. This 1985 study does not represent every subsequent argument.
sources.reviewed: Bibliography checked with Cambridge. Conclusion summary is explicitly indirect, through the cited video.

sources.summary: Collects studies of Isaiah 53 in Jewish and Christian interpretation. McClellan introduces this volume at 7:47. The collection provides a route to broader study of the passage’s interpretation.

sources.title: The Servant-Messiah and the Messiah’s Servants in Targum Jonathan Isaiah
sources.author: William A. Tooman
sources.year: 2021 · in Isaiah’s Servants in Early Judaism and Christianity
sources.summary: Tooman compares the traditional Hebrew text with the Isaiah Targum. The Targum presents a victorious Messiah who protects those who suffer. Its servants are the righteous who obey Torah, God’s instruction. They can include outsiders who join the covenant. This changes how the servant and the community relate. McClellan cites the chapter at 9:17.
sources.limitations: The university repository provides an accessible manuscript. Its pagination can differ from the published chapter. The argument concerns this Targum’s interpretation, not every Jewish reading of Isaiah. The university dates publication to 2021, despite the video’s approximate recollection of its age.
sources.reviewed: Repository manuscript and University of St Andrews publication record reviewed.

sources.title: The Annals of Sennacherib — free English translation
sources.author: Daniel David Luckenbill · University of Chicago
sources.summary: The university provides the full edition as a free PDF. It includes an English translation, transliteration, and copies of the cuneiform signs. The Chicago Prism’s Hezekiah passage is in column III, on printed pages 32–34 (PDF pages 46–48). Sennacherib claims 46 fortified cities, captives, and tribute. He describes Hezekiah confined in Jerusalem. He does not claim to have captured Jerusalem.
sources.limitations: This 1924 translation uses older language and includes uncertain readings. Royal claims and numerical totals are not independent counts. The inscription does not confirm Isaiah’s account of an angel or the number of Assyrian deaths.

sources.title: The Roads and Highways of Ancient Israel
sources.author: David A. Dorsey
sources.summary: Dorsey reconstructs the road network west of the Jordan during the Iron Age. He uses terrain, settlement patterns, written evidence, gates, passes, and later road remains.
sources.limitations: The reconstruction combines evidence from about 1200–587 BCE. Most routes cannot be dated only to Isaiah’s lifetime, and an approximate corridor does not identify every surviving roadbed.
sources.license: Linked reading; route corridors independently redrawn and summarized for this study guide. The published maps and text are not reproduced.

sources.limitations: The road map is a broad historical reconstruction. It does not give a surveyed network for one year in the eighth century BCE.
sources.license: Linked reading; route corridors independently redrawn and summarized for this study guide. The published maps and text are not reproduced.

sources.title: The King’s Road — the imperial communication network
sources.author: Karen Radner
sources.summary: Radner describes the Neo-Assyrian state road and relay network. Her route example crosses the Euphrates at Til Barsip, passes Harran, Guzana, and Nasibina, and reaches the Tigris at Nineveh.
sources.limitations: The essay identifies major crossings and stations. This study guide connects them as a broad corridor and does not claim a surveyed roadbed between each station.
sources.license: Linked academic reading from Oracc and the University of Pennsylvania; corridor independently redrawn and summarized for this study guide.

sources.title: The Roads from and to Aleppo: Some Historical-geographical Considerations in Light of New Archaeological Data
sources.author: Roswitha Del Fabbro
sources.summary: Del Fabbro combines ancient texts, terrain, archaeological survey, and satellite imagery to study the routes around Aleppo. The study traces an Assyrian approach from Nineveh through the upper Habur and Balih regions to the Euphrates, then west toward Aleppo.
sources.limitations: Some sections have stronger textual and archaeological support than others. Long-distance connections are corridors, and local tracks changed across the long period discussed.
sources.license: Linked academic reading; corridor lines independently redrawn and summarized for this study guide. Published maps are not reproduced.

sources.title: Kalhu, Tiglatpileser’s royal residence city

sources.limitations: The source establishes the principal connections, not every bend or station. The eastward and southern continuation is therefore shown as a probable corridor.

passages.title: Worship and justice
passages.summary: Judah has turned away from God. God asks the people to stop doing wrong. He tells them to help people in need. God also gives them hope.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How can worship help you care for others?

studyNotes.title: Ann Madsen on three images of an isolated city
studyNotes.text: Latter-day Saint Isaiah scholar Ann N. Madsen explains in an interview that Isaiah 1:8 uses related images to develop one idea. A temporary field shelter and a city under siege show different aspects of Zion’s isolation. The lines build meaning through comparison, not end rhyme.
studyNotes.application: Read verses 7–9 together. The images follow the account of ruined land; the surviving city remains exposed. Survival here does not mean safety.

passages.title: Nations learn peace
passages.summary: People from many lands come to learn from God. They turn swords into farm tools. God warns them not to trust pride, wealth, or idols.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How can God’s ways change how you treat people?

studyNotes.title: Hopkin: compare the wording before the commentary
studyNotes.text: Hopkin puts the scripture texts first. Parallel columns let readers see differences directly, while brief notes help with difficult points.
studyNotes.application: Compare Isaiah 2:16 in the King James Version with 2 Nephi 12:16. Both name ships of Tarshish. The Book of Mormon also names ships of the sea. Mark the extra clause, then read verses 12–17: the list leads to the humbling of human pride. This example applies Hopkin’s method; he does not discuss this verse in the interview.

passages.title: Leadership and responsibility
passages.summary: Judah loses its good leaders. Some leaders hurt poor people. God calls them to answer for what they did.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How should leaders care for poor people?

passages.title: Cleansing and shelter
passages.summary: God makes Jerusalem clean. He stays with the people who are left. A cloud, fire, and shelter show his care.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How does God clean and guard his people?

passages.title: The vineyard and its fruit
passages.summary: God’s people are like a vineyard. God wants good fruit, such as fair and kind acts. He finds harm instead.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: What good fruit can you grow in your town?

passages.title: Isaiah's call
passages.summary: Isaiah sees the Lord. God makes Isaiah clean. Isaiah then agrees to do a hard job for God.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How does God help Isaiah answer his call?

studyNotes.title: Ann Madsen on Isaiah’s offer to serve
studyNotes.text: Latter-day Saint Isaiah scholar Ann N. Madsen explains in an interview that hineni in Isaiah 6:8 expresses readiness to serve. Isaiah offers himself for the mission; he does more than announce his presence.
studyNotes.application: Trace the sequence in verses 5–8: Isaiah admits his unclean lips, receives cleansing, then volunteers. His offer follows the removal of guilt. Read the reply as a response to that cleansing.

passages.title: Ahaz faces a threat
passages.summary: Two kings plan to attack Judah. Isaiah tells King Ahaz not to fear. God gives a sign called Immanuel.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: What does fear do to Ahaz’s trust?

passages.title: Signs and competing voices
passages.summary: Assyria is coming like a flood. Isaiah tells the people to fear God, not their foes. He warns them about false guides.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Who do you listen to when you feel afraid?

passages.title: Light and a just ruler
passages.summary: A great light shines on people in pain. A child will rule with peace and justice. The chapter also warns proud leaders.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: What kind of hope does a just ruler bring?

passages.title: Assyria and the remnant
passages.summary: Assyria harms many lands and grows proud. God says its power will end. A small group of God’s people will return.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How can success make a person proud?

passages.title: A ruler from Jesse's line
passages.summary: A new ruler comes from Jesse’s family. God’s Spirit rests on him. He rules with justice and brings peace.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How does this ruler care for poor people?

passages.title: Songs of salvation
passages.summary: The people thank God for saving them. They trust him and are not afraid. They tell others what God has done.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How can you share your thanks to God?

passages.title: Judgment on Babylon
passages.summary: God warns proud Babylon. A great attack will bring the city down. Its fall shows that human power does not last.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Why does human power fail?

passages.title: A fallen king
passages.summary: Israel sings about the fall of Babylon’s king. His pride brought him down. The chapter also warns Assyria and Philistia.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: What does pride do to a ruler?

passages.title: Mourning for Moab
passages.summary: Towns in Moab fall. People cry and run away. Isaiah feels grief for them.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How should we act when other people hurt? The linked Come, Follow Me lesson covers nearby chapters. This question is a study guide reflection, not a claim that the lesson teaches this chapter.

passages.title: Refuge and Moab's pride
passages.summary: Moab asks for a safe place. The chapter calls for a fair ruler. It also warns Moab about pride.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Why do proud people still need help? The linked Come, Follow Me lesson covers nearby chapters. This question is a study guide reflection, not a claim that the lesson teaches this chapter.

passages.title: Damascus and Israel
passages.summary: Damascus and Israel lose their power. A few people live. They learn to look to God, not things they made.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: What changes when people look to God? The linked Come, Follow Me lesson covers nearby chapters. This question is a study guide reflection, not a claim that the lesson teaches this chapter.

passages.title: Messengers from Cush
passages.summary: Fast messengers cross the land. God waits and watches. At the end, people bring a gift to Zion.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: What can you learn when God seems to wait? The linked Come, Follow Me lesson covers nearby chapters. This question is a study guide reflection, not a claim that the lesson teaches this chapter.

passages.title: Egypt, Assyria, and Israel
passages.summary: Egypt faces fear, fights, and hunger. Later, Egypt turns to God. Egypt, Assyria, and Israel share God’s gift.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How can God bring old foes together? The linked Come, Follow Me lesson covers nearby chapters. This question is a study guide reflection, not a claim that the lesson teaches this chapter.

passages.title: A sign against reliance on Egypt
passages.summary: Isaiah acts out a warning. Egypt and Cush will be taken away. People learn that these nations cannot save them.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: What may look safe but fail later? The linked Come, Follow Me lesson covers nearby chapters. This question is a study guide reflection, not a claim that the lesson teaches this chapter.

passages.title: Watchmen and warnings
passages.summary: A guard watches for news. He says that Babylon has fallen. The chapter also tells people to help those who flee war.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How can you watch and also help? The linked Come, Follow Me lesson covers nearby chapters. This question is a study guide reflection, not a claim that the lesson teaches this chapter.

passages.title: Jerusalem under scrutiny
passages.summary: Jerusalem gets ready for war but forgets God. The people feast when they should turn back. God also gives Eliakim a key and a new job.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How can you plan and still trust God?

passages.title: Tyre and the sea trade
passages.summary: Tyre grows rich through sea trade. Then its trade fails. The chapter asks how wealth should be used.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How should people use wealth? The linked Come, Follow Me lesson covers nearby chapters. This question is a study guide reflection, not a claim that the lesson teaches this chapter.

passages.title: The earth brought low
passages.summary: The whole earth feels God’s judgment. Joy ends because people break faith with God. God will rule from Zion.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How do broken promises hurt a town?

passages.title: A feast and the end of death
passages.summary: God makes a feast for all people. He ends death, tears, and shame. He also brings proud Moab down.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Who is welcome at God’s feast?

passages.title: Trust while waiting
passages.summary: Judah sings about trust. The people still feel pain and wait for justice. They also hope that the dead will live.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How can hope and pain exist together?

passages.title: A vineyard restored
passages.summary: God guards his vineyard. It grows fruit again. God gathers his people back to worship him.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How is this vineyard unlike the one in chapter 5?

passages.title: A foundation and false security
passages.summary: Proud leaders trust lies. God offers a firm stone as a safe base. A farmer shows that God works in more than one way.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: What makes a base safe and strong?

passages.title: Jerusalem and hidden counsel
passages.summary: Jerusalem faces danger. The people honor God with words, but not with their hearts. God promises that they will see and hear again.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How can words of worship become empty?

passages.title: An alliance and an invitation
passages.summary: Judah runs to Egypt for help. God asks the people to rest and trust him. They refuse, but God still offers mercy.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Why can quiet trust feel hard?

studyNotes.title: Ann Madsen on hearing and following guidance
studyNotes.text: Latter-day Saint Isaiah scholar Ann N. Madsen reads the guiding voice in Isaiah 30:21 as an example of personal revelation during an interview. Her LDS application connects hearing God’s direction with following it.
studyNotes.application: Read verses 19–22 together. Guidance comes amid distress, and the people then reject their idols. In this passage, listening leads to a change in worship and conduct. Madsen’s personal application builds on this address to Judah.

passages.title: Horses cannot save
passages.summary: Egypt’s horses cannot save Judah. Human strength cannot take God’s place. God asks his people to return.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: What good things can become false gods? The linked Come, Follow Me lesson covers nearby chapters. This question is a study guide reflection, not a claim that the lesson teaches this chapter.

passages.title: Justice and peace
passages.summary: A good king rules with justice. God’s Spirit changes the land. Justice brings peace and safe homes.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Why does true peace need justice? The linked Come, Follow Me lesson covers nearby chapters. This question is a study guide reflection, not a claim that the lesson teaches this chapter.

passages.title: Help in a time of danger
passages.summary: The people ask God for help. Roads are empty, and peace deals are broken. God promises safety, justice, and pardon.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How can people live close to a holy God? The linked Come, Follow Me lesson covers nearby chapters. This question is a study guide reflection, not a claim that the lesson teaches this chapter.

passages.title: Judgment pictured through Edom
passages.summary: God judges Edom and other nations. The poem shows fire and empty land. These pictures show that proud power ends.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: What do the empty cities teach about power? The linked Come, Follow Me lesson covers nearby chapters. This question is a study guide reflection, not a claim that the lesson teaches this chapter.

passages.title: A road home
passages.summary: The dry land blooms. Weak people grow strong. A safe road brings God’s people home with joy.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How do healing and coming home fit together?

passages.title: The Assyrian crisis
passages.summary: Assyria captures Judah’s fortified towns. An Assyrian official then travels from Lachish to confront Jerusalem. Assyrian palace reliefs also show Lachish.
passages.dateLabel: 701 BCE · campaign setting
passages.uncertainty: The campaign took place in 701 BCE. The map connects the cities named in the passage. The exact route is unknown.

lds.text: Read Hezekiah’s crisis as an invitation to trust God while facing a real political danger. Church teaching treats the historical setting as the background for that spiritual question.

studyNotes.title: See the Assyrian evidence
studyNotes.text: Isaiah 36:2 places the Assyrian mission at Lachish. A palace relief depicts Sennacherib receiving its spoils. The prism gives a royal account of the campaign. Open the footnotes to see both objects and their source summaries.

passages.title: A battle over trust
passages.summary: The Assyrian speaker challenges trust in Egypt, Hezekiah, and Judah’s God. He speaks to the people on the wall. He promises food but also describes moving them to another land.
passages.dateLabel: 701 BCE · narrative setting
passages.uncertainty: Isaiah records these speeches as part of the account. No separate record from the campaign confirms their exact words.

lds.text: The repeated question of whom to trust can be read alongside Hezekiah’s leadership. Condie’s conference talk applies his example to communities choosing change.

passages.title: The letter and the prayer
passages.summary: Hezekiah takes the threatening message to the temple. His prayer names Assyria’s victories and declares that Judah’s God is the Creator.
passages.dateLabel: 701 BCE · narrative setting
passages.uncertainty: The passage explains the events through faith in God. It does not provide separate historical proof of how Jerusalem survived.

lds.text: Hezekiah’s prayer offers a faithful model for turning toward God in distress. This is a devotional reading of the narrative, alongside the evidence discussed in Historical mode.

studyNotes.title: Compare the accounts of Jerusalem
studyNotes.text: Isaiah credits God with saving Jerusalem. Sennacherib’s account emphasizes Judah’s losses and tribute. It does not claim Jerusalem’s capture. These sources do not establish the same explanation for the outcome.

passages.title: Jerusalem survives
passages.summary: Isaiah compares the survivors to a plant that takes root again. His account credits God with saving Jerusalem. Assyrian accounts describe a royal victory.
passages.dateLabel: 701 BCE · main crisis
passages.uncertainty: The sources give different explanations. The app cannot confirm the exact battle route or the number of deaths.

lds.text: LDS teaching reads the city’s preservation as an expression of God’s power to deliver. The remnant image also invites reflection on renewal after devastation.

passages.title: A later death closes the story
passages.summary: The chapter ends with Sennacherib’s death in his own land. Many years pass between his return home and his death.
passages.dateLabel: 681 BCE · later aftermath
passages.uncertainty: This verse should not be dated to the same night or year as the 701 BCE crisis.

lds.text: A faithful reading sees the ending as fulfillment of the earlier prophecy. The timeline shows the years between these events.

passages.title: Illness and a sign
passages.summary: Hezekiah becomes ill. God promises to save him and the city. Verse 6 shows why chapter order may differ from the order of events.
passages.dateLabel: Around the Assyrian crisis · date uncertain
passages.uncertainty: The map uses 701 BCE to show the setting. The date of Hezekiah’s illness is uncertain.

lds.text: The Lord’s promise to hear prayer offers hope in times of need. Hezekiah’s recovery does not promise the same outcome for every illness.

passages.title: Hezekiah’s song after recovery
passages.summary: The poem moves through images of Sheol, a tent, a loom, birds, and the pit. It ends with living people praising God and passing faithfulness to their children.
passages.dateLabel: Hezekiah’s lifetime · exact date unknown
passages.uncertainty: The poem appears in Isaiah 38, but its exact date is unknown. The map shows Jerusalem as its setting.

lds.text: Church teaching uses this passage to discuss suffering, mercy, and forgiveness. The poem offers ideas for reflection. It does not promise physical recovery for everyone.

passages.title: Babylon and Judah’s future
passages.summary: Visitors from Babylon meet Hezekiah. Isaiah warns that Babylon will later take the palace wealth and the king’s descendants. McClellan’s authorship overview contrasts this warning of exile with the exile already assumed in Isaiah 40. He presents this shift as evidence for later composition of Isaiah 40–55, often called Second Isaiah.
passages.dateLabel: Late eighth century BCE · embassy date debated
passages.uncertainty: The map uses 703 BCE to show the setting. The visit’s exact date is uncertain. Chapter order does not prove the visit followed the 701 BCE crisis. Select 597 or 587/586 BCE to study later events.

lds.text: The Church manual reads these chapters as a transition from Assyrian danger to Babylonian captivity. Consider the contrast between present security and responsibility for future generations.

passages.title: Comfort and renewed strength
passages.summary: God speaks comfort to Jerusalem. People grow tired, but God does not. He gives new strength to those who trust him.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How does God help people who feel forgotten?

passages.title: Do not fear
passages.summary: God tells Israel not to fear. He calls Israel his servant. He will hold and help his people.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How does God’s help change fear?

passages.title: A servant who brings justice
passages.summary: God’s servant brings justice with care. He does not crush weak people. God also tells his people to see and hear.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How can a gentle person still be strong?

passages.title: Called by name
passages.summary: God calls Israel by name. He stays with his people through water and fire. He makes a new path in the desert.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How does an old rescue give new hope?

passages.title: The Creator and the idol maker
passages.summary: People make an idol from the same wood they burn. The idol cannot save them. God names Cyrus as a ruler who will help Jerusalem.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Why can things we make not save us?

passages.title: Cyrus and the LORD's purpose
passages.summary: God gives Cyrus a job, though Cyrus does not know him. God rules over all lands. He asks all people to turn to him.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Who can God use to do his work?

passages.title: The God who carries
passages.summary: People must carry Babylon’s gods. God says he will carry his people all their lives. He alone can save.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: What does it mean for God to carry you?

passages.title: Babylon brought down
passages.summary: Babylon is like a queen who loses her throne. Her pride and magic cannot save her. God holds her to account.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How can pride hide our wrong acts?

passages.title: Leaving Babylon
passages.summary: God asks Israel to listen. He tells the people to leave Babylon. He will care for them on the way.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: What can keep you from listening to God?

passages.title: A servant and remembered Zion
passages.summary: God’s servant has a task for all nations. Zion thinks God forgot her. God says his care is stronger than a mother’s care.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How does God answer Zion’s fear?

passages.title: A listening servant
passages.summary: God’s servant listens before he speaks. He helps tired people and trusts God through pain. Others trust their own light.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How does listening help you serve?

passages.title: Remember and awaken
passages.summary: God tells the people to remember Abraham and Sarah. Old acts of rescue give them hope. Jerusalem’s pain will end.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How can old stories give new hope?

passages.title: Good news for Zion
passages.summary: A messenger brings good news to Zion. He tells of peace, rescue, and God’s rule. The people are called to leave and be clean.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Why is this news good?

passages.title: The suffering servant
passages.summary: People first reject God’s servant. Then they see his pain in a new way. He suffers for others and is honored in the end.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How does this chapter help you think about Jesus?

passages.title: A covenant of peace
passages.summary: Zion feels like a wife left alone. God promises love and peace. He will build the city again and guard its people.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How do these family pictures show love?

passages.title: An invitation without price
passages.summary: God offers free food and drink to thirsty people. He asks them to listen and live. His word will do its work.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: What good gifts can we not buy?

passages.title: A house of prayer for all peoples
passages.summary: God welcomes people who once felt left out. His house is for all people who keep his covenant. He also warns bad leaders.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Who is welcome in God’s house?

passages.title: False worship and healing
passages.summary: The people worship false gods. Yet God stays near humble people who are sorry. He offers healing and peace.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: Why does God come near humble people?

passages.title: The fast God chooses
passages.summary: The people fast but still hurt others. God asks them to feed, house, and clothe people in need. Such care brings light.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How can care for others make worship real?

passages.title: Justice lost and a redeemer promised
passages.summary: Lies and violence push people away from God. The people admit their shared sin. God comes to save and judge.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How can a group admit that it did wrong?

passages.title: Zion receives light
passages.summary: God’s light rises over Zion. Nations and lost children come to the city. God gives it peace and lasting light.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How can God’s light help you serve?

passages.title: Good news and restored lives
passages.summary: God’s chosen servant brings good news. He helps poor, hurt, and trapped people. Ruined places will be built again.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How does Jesus bring good news and care?

passages.title: A new name for Zion
passages.summary: Zion gets a new name. It is no longer left alone. Watchmen pray as a road is made ready for the people.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How can a new name give hope?

passages.title: Judgment and remembered mercy
passages.summary: A warrior comes after judgment. Then the people recall God’s past love and help. They ask him to return.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How can prayer hold pain and hope?

passages.title: A prayer for God's return
passages.summary: The people ask God to come down. They admit their sin. They call God their Father and the maker who shapes clay.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: What does the clay picture teach about God?

passages.title: Judgment and new creation
passages.summary: God judges those who fight him. He blesses his servants. He promises a new world with joy, homes, good work, and peace.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: What parts of life will God make new?

passages.title: Humility, comfort, and all nations
passages.summary: God values humble people who listen to him. He comforts Zion and judges evil. The book ends with all nations coming to worship.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

lds.text: How do comfort and judgment fit together?

events.title: Early eighth-century setting
events.summary: Judah and Israel face the growing power of Assyria. This date shows an earlier setting. It does not mark one event.
events.uncertainty: 780 BCE marks the timeline’s viewing boundary, not Isaiah’s birth or a campaign.

events.title: The northern kingdom falls
events.summary: The speaker in Isaiah 36 uses Samaria’s defeat as a warning. Assyria took the city, faced another revolt, and strengthened its control.
events.uncertainty: 722/721 BCE refers to several stages of conquest and control. Scholars differ on the dates of these stages.

events.title: A new Assyrian king
events.summary: Sargon II dies and Sennacherib succeeds him. Subject states contest Assyrian power.
events.uncertainty: The year helps place the event in time. Map routes and areas are approximate.

events.title: Babylon challenges Assyria
events.summary: Sennacherib defeats Merodach-baladan in Babylonia, providing context for the ruler named in Isaiah 39.
events.uncertainty: The year helps place the event in time. Map routes and areas are approximate.

events.title: Sennacherib’s western campaign
events.summary: The Assyrian campaign reaches Judah. Compare the narrative, the royal inscriptions, and the Lachish reliefs.
events.uncertainty: The year helps place the event in time. Map routes and areas are approximate.

events.title: Palace reliefs show Lachish
events.summary: The palace reliefs present the conquest for an Assyrian royal audience. The artifact was made after the event it depicts.
events.uncertainty: 695 BCE is a display position within the museum’s dating range of 700–692 BCE.

events.title: Sennacherib’s reign ends
events.summary: The later death at the end of Isaiah 37 extends the narrative beyond the invasion year.
events.uncertainty: The year helps place the event in time. Map routes and areas are approximate.

events.title: Nineveh falls
events.summary: The fall of Nineveh weakens Assyrian power. Some Assyrian forces continue to resist.
events.uncertainty: The year helps place the event in time. Map routes and areas are approximate.

events.title: Babylon gains power in the west
events.summary: The battle at Carchemish helps Babylon gain power in the eastern Mediterranean region.
events.uncertainty: The year helps place the event in time. Map routes and areas are approximate.

events.title: Jerusalem and royal deportation
events.summary: Babylon captures Jerusalem and takes its king into exile. These later events help explain the warning in Isaiah 39.
events.uncertainty: The year helps place the event in time. Map routes and areas are approximate.

events.title: Jerusalem and the temple destroyed
events.summary: Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the temple. This event occurs long after the Assyrian crisis.
events.uncertainty: Scholars date the destruction to 587 or 586 BCE. The app shows both dates.

events.title: Persia takes Babylon
events.summary: Cyrus conquers Babylon. The Cyrus Cylinder describes his support for restoring worship. It does not mention the return of Judah’s exiles.
events.uncertainty: The year helps place the event in time. Map routes and areas are approximate.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.summary: Jerusalem was Judah’s capital and the home of its royal court and temple. Its ridge-top position made it defensible but not isolated.
places.detail: Jerusalem is the political and spiritual center of Isaiah’s world. Assyrian pressure, royal policy, temple worship, judgment, and hope all meet here.

places.name: Lachish
places.summary: Lachish was a major fortified city southwest of Jerusalem. It guarded roads through Judah’s western lowlands.
places.detail: Assyria’s capture of Lachish exposed Jerusalem to direct attack. Its fall shows how much of Judah was lost even though the capital survived.

places.name: Nineveh
places.summary: Nineveh became Sennacherib’s royal capital on the Tigris. Its palaces displayed Assyrian wealth, building, and military victories.
places.detail: Nineveh represents the imperial power that threatened Judah. It also preserves Assyrian art and inscriptions that can be compared with Isaiah’s account.

places.name: Babylon
places.summary: Babylon was a major city on the Euphrates and a center of southern Mesopotamian power. Its kings often competed with Assyria before Babylon became an empire.
places.detail: In Isaiah, Babylon changes from a rival inside Assyria’s world to the power linked with Judah’s future exile. It later becomes the setting from which restoration is announced.

places.name: Samaria
places.summary: Samaria was the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel. Assyria captured it and deported part of its population.
places.detail: Samaria’s fall showed Judah what Assyrian conquest could do to a neighboring kingdom. Isaiah treats that disaster as both a warning and part of the region’s political upheaval.

places.name: Hamath
places.summary: Hamath was an important kingdom and city on the Orontes in western Syria. It stood on routes between inland Syria and the Mediterranean coast.
places.detail: Assyria’s defeat of Hamath made it a warning to other western kingdoms. Isaiah uses such fallen cities to expose the empire’s argument that resistance is useless.

places.name: Arpad
places.summary: Arpad was a north Syrian city-state near Aleppo. Assyria fought repeated campaigns there before making it part of the empire.
places.detail: Arpad’s long resistance ended in Assyrian conquest. Its defeat became part of Assyria’s political message to cities such as Jerusalem.

places.name: Harran
places.summary: Harran was a trading and religious center on routes across northern Mesopotamia. Its position linked Assyria, Syria, and Anatolia.
places.detail: Harran shows the reach of Assyrian control far beyond Judah. Isaiah includes conquered northern cities in the empire’s attempt to intimidate Jerusalem.

places.name: Gozan
places.summary: Gozan is usually linked with Guzana at Tell Halaf. It became an Assyrian provincial center in northern Mesopotamia.
places.detail: Gozan became part of the Assyrian system of provinces and deportation. Its name helps Isaiah’s readers feel the scale of Assyria’s earlier conquests.

places.name: Libnah
places.summary: Libnah was a fortified town in Judah’s western lowlands. Its exact site remains uncertain.
places.uncertainty: This is a representative location. Competing site identifications exist; the coordinate does not settle them.
places.detail: Libnah matters because the Assyrian campaign did not stop at Lachish. Its uncertain location also warns against drawing a precise military route from the text.

places.name: Tyre
places.summary: Tyre was a wealthy Phoenician port with an island center. Its merchants connected the Levant with Mediterranean trade.
places.detail: Isaiah uses the Phoenician trade world to show that wealth and international reach do not make a city secure. These ports also show how Judah belonged to a larger economic world.

places.name: Sidon
places.summary: Sidon was a major Phoenician port north of Tyre. Its ships and workshops formed part of a wide Mediterranean trade network.
places.detail: Isaiah uses the Phoenician trade world to show that wealth and international reach do not make a city secure. These ports also show how Judah belonged to a larger economic world.

places.name: Ashkelon
places.summary: Ashkelon was a fortified Philistine port on the southern coast. Trade routes and armies passed through its region.
places.detail: Philistine cities stood between Judah and Egypt on the main coastal road. Their revolts and alliances drew Assyria toward Judah’s border.

places.name: Ekron
places.summary: Ekron was a large Philistine city with strong olive-oil production. Its rulers balanced local interests against Assyrian demands.
places.detail: Philistine cities stood between Judah and Egypt on the main coastal road. Their revolts and alliances drew Assyria toward Judah’s border.

places.name: Memphis · Egypt
places.summary: Memphis was a major city near the head of the Nile Delta. It was a political and religious center of Egypt.
places.detail: Egypt and Cush offered an alternative to Assyrian power. Isaiah repeatedly asks whether Judah should trust that alliance or trust God.

places.name: Damascus
places.summary: Damascus was the capital of Aram-Damascus and an important inland trade center. It controlled routes through southern Syria.
places.detail: Damascus joined Israel against Judah before it fell to Assyria. Its rise and defeat show how small kingdoms formed coalitions under imperial pressure.

places.name: Carchemish
places.summary: Carchemish was a fortified city at a major Euphrates crossing. Armies and trade routes moved through this strategic point.
places.detail: The later Babylonian victory at Carchemish shifted control of Syria and the Levant away from Egypt. That change helps explain the Babylonian future anticipated in Isaiah.

places.name: Susa
places.summary: A city east of Babylon that helps show the Persian setting. Isaiah does not describe an event at Susa.
places.detail: Susa belongs to the Persian horizon that follows Babylon. Persia’s rise provides the political setting for Isaiah’s promises connected with Cyrus.

places.name: Aiath
places.summary: Aiath was a town north of Jerusalem. Its exact identification remains debated.
places.detail: Isaiah uses this chain of towns to picture an army moving toward Jerusalem. The names make the Assyrian threat feel closer at each step.

places.name: Anathoth
places.summary: Anathoth was a small town a few miles northeast of Jerusalem. It belonged to the territory of Benjamin.
places.detail: Isaiah uses this chain of towns to picture an army moving toward Jerusalem. The names make the Assyrian threat feel closer at each step.

places.name: Ar
places.summary: Ar was an important settlement in Moab. Its exact site is uncertain.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Arnon
places.summary: The Arnon is the deep gorge now called Wadi Mujib. It cut across Moab and formed a major natural boundary.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Aroer
places.summary: Aroer was a settlement east of the Jordan. More than one ancient place used this name.
places.detail: Aroer helps locate the borderlands east of Israel. Isaiah uses abandoned towns there to show the reach of regional collapse.

places.name: Ashdod
places.summary: Ashdod was a fortified Philistine city near the Mediterranean coast. It controlled rich farmland and access to coastal trade.
places.detail: Philistine cities stood between Judah and Egypt on the main coastal road. Their revolts and alliances drew Assyria toward Judah’s border.

places.name: Assyria
places.summary: Assyria was an empire centered in northern Mesopotamia. Its armies, governors, tribute system, and deportations reshaped the Levant.
places.detail: Assyria is the dominant geopolitical force in much of Isaiah 1–39. The book presents it as both a human empire and an instrument whose violence and pride are judged.

places.name: Bashan
places.summary: Bashan was a fertile upland east of the Sea of Galilee. It was known for forests, pasture, and strong cattle.
places.detail: Bashan’s famous strength and fertility make it a useful image of human grandeur. Isaiah places such grandeur under God’s judgment.

places.name: Beer-elim
places.summary: Beer-elim was a Moabite location known from the biblical text. Its exact site is uncertain.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Bozrah
places.summary: Bozrah was a chief city of Edom in the highlands southeast of Judah. It stood near routes through the Arabah and Transjordan.
places.detail: Edom was Judah’s neighbor and frequent rival. Isaiah uses its land to speak about regional judgment and the reversal of power.

places.name: Calneh
places.summary: Calneh was a north Syrian city associated with the region of Arpad. Its exact identification is debated.
places.detail: Calneh belongs to the list of cities Assyria claimed to have overcome. The comparison turns geography into imperial propaganda aimed at Jerusalem.

places.name: Cush
places.summary: Cush was the kingdom south of Egypt, centered in Nubia. Cushite rulers also governed Egypt during part of Isaiah’s lifetime.
places.detail: Egypt and Cush offered an alternative to Assyrian power. Isaiah repeatedly asks whether Judah should trust that alliance or trust God.

places.name: Cyprus
places.summary: Cyprus was a large Mediterranean island with ports, copper resources, and wide trade links. Biblical Kittim often points toward Cyprus and the western sea.
places.detail: Isaiah uses the Phoenician trade world to show that wealth and international reach do not make a city secure. These ports also show how Judah belonged to a larger economic world.

places.name: Dedan
places.summary: Dedan was an oasis and caravan center in northwestern Arabia. Traders carried incense and other goods through this region.
places.detail: Arabian routes carried goods, news, and refugees across the desert. Isaiah uses these peoples to widen the story beyond Judah and the great empires.

places.name: Dibon
places.summary: Dibon was a prominent Moabite city east of the Dead Sea. It stood near the King’s Highway and controlled nearby farmland.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Edom
places.summary: Edom occupied the highlands south and southeast of the Dead Sea. Its territory controlled routes between Judah, Arabia, and the Red Sea.
places.detail: Edom was Judah’s neighbor and frequent rival. Isaiah uses its land to speak about regional judgment and the reversal of power.

places.name: Egypt
places.summary: Egypt was an old kingdom centered on the Nile. Its wealth and armies made it a possible ally and a rival great power.
places.detail: Egypt and Cush offered an alternative to Assyrian power. Isaiah repeatedly asks whether Judah should trust that alliance or trust God.

places.name: Elam
places.summary: Elam was a kingdom east of Babylonia in southwestern Iran. It sometimes allied with Babylon against Assyria.
places.detail: This place helps show how Isaiah’s world connected small kingdoms, trade routes, and competing empires.

places.name: Elealeh
places.summary: Elealeh was a Moabite town on the plateau east of the Dead Sea. It lay close to Heshbon.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Euphrates
places.summary: The Euphrates was the great river running from Anatolia through Syria and Mesopotamia. Major cities and imperial routes followed its valley.
places.detail: The Euphrates often marks the direction from which Mesopotamian empires reached Syria and Judah. Isaiah uses its floodwaters as an image of Assyria’s overwhelming advance.

places.name: Galilee
places.summary: Galilee was the northern region around the Sea of Galilee. It lay near international roads and was exposed to invasion from the north.
places.detail: Galilee was among the first Israelite regions to suffer Assyrian conquest. Isaiah turns this exposed borderland into a setting for renewed hope.

places.name: Geba
places.summary: Geba was a Benjaminite town north of Jerusalem. It stood near a pass through the central hill country.
places.detail: Isaiah uses this chain of towns to picture an army moving toward Jerusalem. The names make the Assyrian threat feel closer at each step.

places.name: Gibeah
places.summary: Gibeah was a Benjaminite hill town just north of Jerusalem. Its elevated position overlooked approaches to the capital.
places.detail: Isaiah uses this chain of towns to picture an army moving toward Jerusalem. The names make the Assyrian threat feel closer at each step.

places.name: Hanes
places.summary: Hanes was an Egyptian center, probably in the Nile Valley. Its exact role and identification in this period remain uncertain.
places.detail: Egypt and Cush offered an alternative to Assyrian power. Isaiah repeatedly asks whether Judah should trust that alliance or trust God.

places.name: Heshbon
places.summary: Heshbon was a major town on the plateau east of the Jordan. It sat near roads linking Ammon, Moab, and the north.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Horonaim
places.summary: Horonaim was a Moabite town, probably near a descent toward the Dead Sea. Its exact location remains uncertain.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Jahaz
places.summary: Jahaz was a settlement on the Moabite plateau. Its precise site remains debated.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Jazer
places.summary: Jazer was a town east of the Jordan near productive fields and vineyards. Its exact site is uncertain.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Kedar
places.summary: Kedar was a confederation of Arabian pastoral and trading groups. Its people moved across routes east and south of the Levant.
places.detail: Arabian routes carried goods, news, and refugees across the desert. Isaiah uses these peoples to widen the story beyond Judah and the great empires.

places.name: Kir-hareseth
places.summary: Kir-hareseth was a major fortified center in Moab, often linked with modern Kerak. It stood above routes south of the Arnon.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Lebanon
places.summary: Lebanon was the mountain region north of Israel, famous for cedar forests. Its timber and passes had economic and strategic value.
places.detail: Isaiah uses Lebanon’s cedars as images of wealth, height, and royal power. Their fall represents the humbling of proud rulers and empires.

places.name: Luhith
places.summary: Luhith was a Moabite site associated with an uphill road. Its precise location is uncertain.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Medeba
places.summary: Medeba was a town on the Moabite plateau east of the Dead Sea. Its surrounding plain supported farming and travel.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Media
places.summary: Media was a kingdom on the Iranian plateau east of Assyria. Median forces later helped Babylon defeat the Assyrian Empire.
places.detail: The Medes helped end Assyrian rule and later became part of the Persian imperial world. Their appearance marks how quickly the balance of power could change.

places.name: Michmash
places.summary: Michmash was a hill town north of Jerusalem near a narrow pass. The pass made it important for travel and defense.
places.detail: Isaiah uses this chain of towns to picture an army moving toward Jerusalem. The names make the Assyrian threat feel closer at each step.

places.name: Midian
places.summary: Midian was a broad region and group of peoples south and east of the Gulf of Aqaba. Its routes connected Arabia with the Levant.
places.detail: Arabian routes carried goods, news, and refugees across the desert. Isaiah uses these peoples to widen the story beyond Judah and the great empires.

places.name: Migron
places.summary: Migron was a site north of Jerusalem near Michmash. Its precise identification is uncertain.
places.detail: Isaiah uses this chain of towns to picture an army moving toward Jerusalem. The names make the Assyrian threat feel closer at each step.

places.name: Moab
places.summary: Moab occupied the plateau east of the Dead Sea. Its towns, farms, and roads lay between Judah, Ammon, Edom, and Arabia.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Mount Carmel
places.summary: Mount Carmel is a wooded ridge reaching the Mediterranean coast. It overlooks the coastal plain and the Jezreel Valley.
places.detail: Carmel’s fertility made its withering a strong image of national disaster. Its recovery could also signal renewed life.

places.name: Mount Seir
places.summary: Mount Seir was the rugged highland associated with Edom. Its ridges controlled routes through the southern Transjordan.
places.detail: Edom was Judah’s neighbor and frequent rival. Isaiah uses its land to speak about regional judgment and the reversal of power.

places.name: Nebo
places.summary: Nebo was a Moabite town and cult center on the plateau east of the Dead Sea. Its exact ancient site is usually placed near Mount Nebo.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Negeb
places.summary: The Negeb was Judah’s dry southern region. Roads through it linked the hill country with Egypt, Edom, and Arabia.
places.detail: The Negeb was a corridor for envoys, tribute, and armies moving toward Egypt. Isaiah uses it when criticizing Judah’s search for Egyptian protection.

places.name: Nile
places.summary: The Nile sustained Egypt’s farms, cities, and transport. Control of its water and harvests supported Egyptian power.
places.detail: Egypt and Cush offered an alternative to Assyrian power. Isaiah repeatedly asks whether Judah should trust that alliance or trust God.

places.name: Nimrim
places.summary: Nimrim was a water-rich location in Moab, often linked with a stream south of the Dead Sea. Its exact identification is uncertain.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Nob
places.summary: Nob was a settlement close to Jerusalem, probably on a northern approach. Its exact location remains uncertain.
places.detail: Isaiah uses this chain of towns to picture an army moving toward Jerusalem. The names make the Assyrian threat feel closer at each step.

places.name: Pathros
places.summary: Pathros means Upper Egypt, the Nile Valley south of the Delta. It was one of Egypt’s main historic regions.
places.detail: Egypt and Cush offered an alternative to Assyrian power. Isaiah repeatedly asks whether Judah should trust that alliance or trust God.

places.name: Philistia
places.summary: Philistia was the coastal plain ruled by cities such as Ashdod, Ashkelon, and Ekron. Its ports and roads made it valuable to larger empires.
places.detail: Philistine cities stood between Judah and Egypt on the main coastal road. Their revolts and alliances drew Assyria toward Judah’s border.

places.name: Ramah
places.summary: Ramah was a Benjaminite town north of Jerusalem. It stood along an important ridge route.
places.detail: Isaiah uses this chain of towns to picture an army moving toward Jerusalem. The names make the Assyrian threat feel closer at each step.

places.name: Rezeph
places.summary: Rezeph was a fortified city on routes across the Syrian desert. It later became an Assyrian provincial center.
places.detail: Rezeph was another city absorbed by Assyria. Its fate strengthens the imperial boast that no local god or king could resist Assyrian power.

places.name: Sela
places.summary: Sela means rock and probably points to a stronghold in the Edomite highlands. Its exact identification is debated.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Sharon
places.summary: Sharon was the fertile coastal plain west of the central hills. Its fields and north-south road gave it economic value.
places.detail: Sharon links the coast with Judah’s hill country. Isaiah uses its fertile landscape to measure both devastation and restoration.

places.name: Sheba
places.summary: Sheba was a wealthy south Arabian kingdom linked with incense and caravan trade. Its merchants connected Arabia with the Levant.
places.detail: Arabian routes carried goods, news, and refugees across the desert. Isaiah uses these peoples to widen the story beyond Judah and the great empires.

places.name: Sibmah
places.summary: Sibmah was a Moabite town known for vineyards. Its exact location near Heshbon is uncertain.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Tema
places.summary: Tema was a major oasis in northern Arabia. It served caravans moving between Arabia, Mesopotamia, and the Levant.
places.detail: Arabian routes carried goods, news, and refugees across the desert. Isaiah uses these peoples to widen the story beyond Judah and the great empires.

places.name: Valley of Achor
places.summary: The Valley of Achor lay near the approaches to Jericho. Its exact extent is uncertain.
places.detail: Isaiah turns this remembered place of trouble into pasture for a restored people. The geography supports the movement from judgment to hope.

places.name: Zoan
places.summary: Zoan, or Tanis, was an important city in the eastern Nile Delta. It was close to routes between Egypt and the Levant.
places.detail: Egypt and Cush offered an alternative to Assyrian power. Isaiah repeatedly asks whether Judah should trust that alliance or trust God.

places.name: Zoar
places.summary: Zoar was a town near the southern end of the Dead Sea. Its exact site is debated.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Brook of the Willows
places.summary: The Brook of the Willows was a stream or wadi on Moab’s border. It is often linked with Wadi al-Hasa.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Eglaim
places.summary: Eglaim was a Moabite location known from the biblical text. Its exact site is uncertain.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Eglath-shelishiyah
places.summary: Eglath-shelishiyah was a place near the southern Dead Sea. Its exact identification is uncertain.
places.detail: Isaiah’s poems about Moab move through towns, fields, and escape routes. Together they show war and displacement spreading across a whole region.

places.name: Javan
places.summary: Javan is the biblical name for Ionia and, more broadly, Greek lands across the sea. It represents the western Mediterranean world.
places.detail: These distant peoples widen Isaiah’s horizon beyond Judah and its immediate enemies. They help frame the book’s final vision as international in scope.

places.name: Lud
places.summary: Lud probably points to Lydia in western Anatolia. It represents a distant people beyond the eastern Mediterranean.
places.detail: These distant peoples widen Isaiah’s horizon beyond Judah and its immediate enemies. They help frame the book’s final vision as international in scope.

places.name: Tubal
places.summary: Tubal was a people and kingdom in Anatolia. Assyrian records place it north of Syria in the mountain lands.
places.detail: These distant peoples widen Isaiah’s horizon beyond Judah and its immediate enemies. They help frame the book’s final vision as international in scope.

places.name: Joppa / Jaffa
places.summary: Joppa, now Jaffa, was a port on the central coast. It connected inland towns with Mediterranean shipping.
places.uncertainty: Representative site coordinates, not the position of an ancient road.
places.detail: Isaiah uses the Phoenician trade world to show that wealth and international reach do not make a city secure. These ports also show how Judah belonged to a larger economic world.

places.name: Timnah · Tel Batash
places.summary: Timnah was a Philistine-border town in the Sorek Valley. Its farmland and road position made it a contested place.
places.uncertainty: Representative site coordinates, not the position of an ancient road.
places.detail: Philistine cities stood between Judah and Egypt on the main coastal road. Their revolts and alliances drew Assyria toward Judah’s border.

places.name: Azekah
places.summary: Azekah was a fortified town above the Elah Valley. It guarded routes from the coastal plain into Judah’s hills.
places.uncertainty: Representative site coordinates, not the position of an ancient road.
places.detail: This place helps show how Isaiah’s world connected small kingdoms, trade routes, and competing empires.

campaigns.title: From Lachish to Jerusalem
campaigns.summary: Isaiah 36:2 sends the Assyrian representative from Lachish to Jerusalem. The connection brings the campaign to the city’s walls.
campaigns.detail: The line connects Lachish and Jerusalem. The passage does not establish the official’s exact road or travel time. It does not trace Sennacherib’s movements. Compare the chapter with the Assyrian reliefs of Lachish.
campaigns.uncertainty: The line connects places in the account. The exact route is unknown.

campaigns.evidence: Named sites · travel order not established
campaigns.uncertainty: Lines connect sites affected by the campaign. They do not trace roads or establish travel order.
campaigns.title: The campaign along the coast
campaigns.summary: The Assyrian account describes the submission of Phoenician centers and attacks on southern coastal towns.
campaigns.detail: Joppa is a named place in the annals. The line replaces an earlier unnamed waypoint. Tyre’s island and mainland settlements must be distinguished; the line does not claim the capture of the island city. The geographic order on this map is not a verified march sequence.

campaigns.title: The Babylonian embassy
campaigns.dateLabel: Late eighth century BCE · exact date debated
campaigns.summary: Isaiah 39 links Babylonian visitors with Hezekiah’s court.
campaigns.detail: The line links the embassy’s origin and destination. Isaiah 39 does not name intermediate stops or establish the visit’s exact year.
campaigns.uncertainty: The line connects the two cities. The travel route and exact date are unknown.

campaigns.title: Exile in Babylon
campaigns.summary: Compare Jerusalem and Babylon to study the later events described in Isaiah 39.
campaigns.detail: The map connects Jerusalem and Babylon. The line does not show one confirmed route into exile. People did not travel continuously throughout this period.
campaigns.uncertainty: The line connects the cities. The exact route into exile is unknown.

campaigns.evidence: Named sites · travel order not established
campaigns.uncertainty: Lines connect sites affected by the campaign. They do not trace roads or establish travel order.
campaigns.title: Timnah and Ekron
campaigns.summary: The annals name the capture of Eltekeh and Timnah, then describe action at Ekron.
campaigns.detail: The map connects the identified sites of Timnah and Ekron. Eltekeh’s location is disputed, so the battle remains in the explanation without a precise map pin. The order in a royal account is not enough to locate the road.

campaigns.evidence: Named sites · travel order not established
campaigns.uncertainty: Lines connect sites affected by the campaign. They do not trace roads or establish travel order.
campaigns.title: Fortified towns of Judah
campaigns.summary: Azekah and Lachish help place the attack on Judah’s fortified towns in the lowlands.
campaigns.detail: The Azekah inscription and the evidence at Lachish concern separate attacks. They do not establish which came first. This connection shows the regional setting of Isaiah 36:1, not a confirmed march from one siege to the other.

regions.name: Land near Babylon · approximate
regions.summary: Babylonia occupied the river plain of southern Mesopotamia, with Babylon as its leading city. Its rulers controlled rich farmland, temples, and trade routes but often faced Assyrian intervention.
regions.uncertainty: The shape does not show a firm border. Rule changed over time. Sennacherib beat Merodach-baladan in 703 BCE. Babylon became the main power in 605 BCE.
regions.detail: Babylon mattered to Isaiah before it became the next great empire. Merodach-baladan challenged Assyria and contacted Hezekiah, making Babylon both a possible ally and a warning about Judah’s future.

regions.name: Land of Judah · approximate
regions.summary: Judah was a small highland kingdom centered on Jerusalem. Its farms, fortified towns, and roads connected the capital with the coastal plain, the Jordan Valley, and the south.
regions.uncertainty: The shape does not show a firm border. Rule changed over time.
regions.detail: Judah stood between larger powers and had to choose between revolt, tribute, and foreign alliances. Isaiah addresses those choices while warning that political plans cannot replace faithful leadership.

regions.name: Philistine city-states · approximate
regions.summary: Philistia consisted of several city-states on the southern coastal plain, including Ashdod, Ashkelon, Ekron, Gaza, and Gath. The cities could act together, compete with one another, or answer to a larger empire.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is schematic. Philistine political control changed by city and year, especially under Assyrian and Babylonian pressure.
regions.detail: Philistia matters in Isaiah because its cities stood on the coastal route between Egypt and the Levant. Its rulers appear in warnings, revolts, alliances, and the Assyrian campaign that also threatened Judah.

regions.name: Egyptian realm · approximate
regions.summary: Egypt controlled the Nile valley and delta. Its divided rulers, armies, horses, and wealth made it an attractive but unreliable political partner for Judah.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is schematic. Egypt’s dynasties and centers of power changed during Isaiah’s setting, and Kushite rulers governed Egypt for part of this period.
regions.detail: Isaiah addresses Egypt both as a major nation in God’s wider purposes and as a warning against misplaced political trust. Chapters 30–31 challenge Judah’s attempt to rely on Egyptian horses and military help.

regions.name: Cushite realm · approximate
regions.summary: Cush was a kingdom south of Egypt in Nubia. Kushite kings also ruled Egypt as its Twenty-fifth Dynasty during part of Isaiah’s historical setting.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is schematic and shows only the northern part of the Kushite sphere. Control changed over time, and the map does not mark a fixed border.
regions.detail: Cush appears in Isaiah as a distant nation, a source of messengers, and part of the conflict between Egypt and Assyria. Isaiah 37 names Tirhakah, usually identified with the Kushite ruler Taharqa.

regions.name: Lands under Assyria · approximate
regions.summary: The Neo-Assyrian Empire expanded from northern Mesopotamia to the Mediterranean and Egypt. It ruled through armies, governors, tribute, local client kings, and forced population movement.
regions.uncertainty: Assyria did not rule all these lands in the same way. Its power also changed over time. The shape does not show a firm border for each year.
regions.detail: Assyria created the central political crisis in much of Isaiah 1–39. Its expansion destroyed Israel, devastated Judah, and forced Jerusalem to decide where it placed its trust.

regions.name: Lands under Babylon · approximate
regions.summary: The Neo-Babylonian Empire replaced Assyria as the main power in Mesopotamia and the Levant. Under Nebuchadnezzar II, Babylon conquered Jerusalem and deported many Judeans.
regions.uncertainty: The shape does not show a firm border. Rule changed over time.
regions.detail: Babylon forms the horizon of Isaiah’s exile and restoration material. It represents both the power that carries Judah away and the empire from which the exiles are later called to depart.

regions.name: Lands under Persia · approximate
regions.summary: The Persian Empire under Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BCE and joined its territories to a much larger realm. Persian kings often governed through existing local institutions and officials.
regions.uncertainty: The shape shows only part of the land Cyrus ruled.
regions.detail: Persia matters because Cyrus’s rise changed the future of displaced Judeans. Isaiah presents him as the ruler who makes Jerusalem’s restoration politically possible.

words.label: King
words.meaning: A ruler. The verse names both Judah’s king and the Assyrian king.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H4428. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: Both rulers have the title king, but their power differs. Later, the speaker calls the Assyrian king “great” to stress his power.

words.label: Hezekiah
words.meaning: The king of Judah in this account.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H2396. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.

words.label: Sennacherib
words.meaning: The Assyrian king named at the opening of the campaign narrative.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H5576. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.

words.label: Assyria
words.meaning: The empire that threatens Judah.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H804. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: The Hebrew names Assyria, while the Greek phrase calls its ruler king of the Assyrians. Both identify the power attacking Judah.

words.label: Judah
words.meaning: The southern kingdom in this passage.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H3063. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: Elsewhere, Judah can name an ancestor, a people, or a territory. Here the references to cities and Jerusalem identify the kingdom.

words.label: Rabshakeh
words.meaning: An Assyrian official’s title. The translation uses an English spelling of its sounds.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H7262. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: Strong’s Hebrew dictionary explains the title Rabshakeh as “chief cupbearer,” an official who served drinks to the king. In Isaiah 36, this official speaks for the Assyrian king and urges Jerusalem to surrender. Here, his role is that of a senior royal representative.

words.label: Lachish
words.meaning: A fortified city of Judah; the starting point of the mission to Jerusalem.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H3923. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.

words.label: Jerusalem
words.meaning: Judah’s royal and temple city.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H3389. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: In Isaiah 36:2, the Hebrew word has an ending that means toward Jerusalem. English expresses this direction with the separate word “to.”

words.label: Army
words.meaning: A military force in this context.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H2426. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: The Hebrew word can mean force or strength. Here it refers to soldiers sent by the king. The Greek word can also mean power or force.

words.label: Aqueduct
words.meaning: A channel that carries water.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H8585. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.

words.label: Pool
words.meaning: A water pool or reservoir.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H1295. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.

words.label: Confidence
words.greekNote: Swete’s text uses πεποιθὼς in verse 4. This verb form expresses trust in a question. It is not a direct noun match for “confidence.”
words.meaning: The reliance or confidence that the speaker challenges.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H986. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: In Isaiah 36:4, the Hebrew noun for confidence and the related verb for trust occur in the same question. This repetition introduces the speech’s repeated challenge: whom can Judah trust?

words.label: Trust
words.greekNote: This form comes from verse 5. The Greek verb has different forms elsewhere in the chapter.
words.meaning: To rely on someone or something.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H982. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: Rabshakeh challenges trust in Egypt’s military help in Isaiah 36:6, 9 and trust in the LORD’s rescue in verse 15. His speech attacks both reasons for resisting Assyria.

words.label: Egypt
words.meaning: The southern power whose help the speaker depicts as unreliable.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H4714. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: The Assyrian speaker compares Egypt to a broken reed. He uses this image to argue that Egypt cannot help Judah.

words.label: Aramaic
words.greekNote: The Greek adverb Συριστί names the language. Its ancient meaning differs from modern national names.
words.meaning: The language the Judean officials ask the envoy to use.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H762. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: The officials ask for Aramaic so the people on the wall cannot understand the discussion. The speaker continues in the people’s language.

words.label: Jews’ language
words.meaning: In Judean: the speech of the local audience, rendered “the Jews’ language” in WEB.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H3066. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: One Hebrew adverb corresponds to the English phrase “the Jews’ language.” In Isaiah 36:13, Rabshakeh uses this language to address the people on the wall directly.

words.label: Remnant
words.greekNote: This Greek form comes from verse 4 and means those left. Verse 32 uses another form. Verse 31 uses different Hebrew wording and has no match in this entry.
words.meaning: Those remaining after disaster or loss.
