words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H7611. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: In Isaiah 37:4, Hezekiah asks for prayer for the survivors. In verses 31–32, roots and fruit describe their future recovery. The image presents survival as the beginning of renewed life.

words.label: Spirit
words.meaning: A spirit or state of mind that God says he will put in the Assyrian king.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H7307. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: The Hebrew word can mean wind, breath, or spirit. Isaiah 37:7 connects it with the Assyrian king hearing news and returning home.

words.label: Shadow
words.meaning: The shadow involved in the sign given to Hezekiah.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H6738. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.

words.label: Steps / sundial
words.meaning: Steps or degrees. Some translations use “sundial” for the structure where the shadow appears.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H4609. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: The World English Bible translates wording about steps as “sundial.” The Hebrew does not specify a circular clock face.

words.label: Sheol
words.meaning: The realm or place of the dead in the poem’s imagery.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H7585. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: Isaiah 38:18–19 contrasts the dead, who cannot praise God, with the living, who can. Hezekiah places his own praise within that contrast after his rescue from death.

related.label: Matthew 16:18 — gates of Hades
related.note: A later verbal/image comparison, not a claim that Matthew directly quotes Isaiah 38.

words.label: Soul / life
words.meaning: The speaker’s life or self, rescued from destruction.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H5315. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: Isaiah 38:17 places rescue from death beside forgiveness of sins. The reference to his soul belongs to Hezekiah’s thanks for his restored life.

words.label: Sins
words.meaning: Wrongdoing that the poem describes as thrown behind God’s back.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H2399. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: Isaiah 38:17 describes God casting the speaker’s sins behind his back. This image expresses forgiveness alongside Hezekiah’s rescue from death.

words.label: Babylon
words.greekNote: This form comes from verse 1. Later verses use other word forms and names for the people.
words.meaning: The city and kingdom of the visitors. Isaiah also names Babylon in his warning about the future.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H894. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: Babylon sends a gift in Isaiah 39:1, but becomes the destination of Judah’s lost treasures in verse 6. The warning concerns the same wealth Hezekiah showed the visitors.

words.label: Eunuchs
words.meaning: Court servants described with a term that can denote eunuchs or officials.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H5631. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: Isaiah 39:7 places Hezekiah’s descendants in the Babylonian king’s palace as servants. The warning reverses their position: members of Judah’s royal family will serve a foreign ruler.

words.label: Peace
words.meaning: Peace or well-being in Hezekiah’s days.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H7965. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: In Isaiah 39:8, Hezekiah speaks of peace in his own days after hearing that his descendants will be taken away. His response contrasts present security with the future loss Isaiah announces.

words.label: Truth / stability
words.greekNote: Swete’s Greek uses δικαιοσύνη, which commonly means righteousness or justice. The Hebrew and Greek words do not have identical meanings.
words.meaning: Reliability or faithfulness, paired with peace.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H571. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: The Hebrew word can mean firmness or faithfulness. Paired with peace in Isaiah 39:8, it can suggest stable conditions during Hezekiah’s lifetime.

words.label: Justice
words.meaning: A just decision or the practice of justice.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H4941. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: The commands that follow concern people who need protection.

words.label: Holy
words.meaning: Holy or sacred.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H6918. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: The threefold repetition belongs to the vision of the Lord and his glory.

words.label: Sign
words.greekNote: This form occurs in verses 11 and 14.
words.meaning: A sign or distinguishing mark.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H226. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: Read the sign with the political threat described earlier in the chapter.

words.label: Remnant
words.meaning: What remains after loss.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H7605. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: The survivors are described as returning to the mighty God.

words.label: Shoot
words.meaning: A twig or shoot.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H2415. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: New growth from Jesse’s stock introduces the image of a renewed ruler.

words.label: Salvation
words.meaning: Deliverance or rescue.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H3444. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: The song joins salvation with trust, strength, and the end of fear.

words.label: Stone
words.meaning: A stone.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H68. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: The construction image describes a reliable foundation in Zion.

words.label: Book
words.meaning: A written document or scroll.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H5612. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: The sealed document illustrates the inability to receive the vision. The ancient object need not be a bound book.

words.label: Rest
words.meaning: Rest or quietness.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H5183. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: The verse contrasts returning and rest with the refusal to trust.

words.label: Wilderness
words.meaning: Open country or wilderness.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H4057. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: The dry landscape becomes a place of joy in the restoration poem.

words.label: Comfort
words.meaning: To comfort or console in this setting.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H5162. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: The repeated command opens the message of comfort to the people.

words.label: Servant
words.meaning: A servant or one who serves.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H5650. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: This servant receives a task concerning justice for the nations. The noun alone does not settle the servant’s identity.

words.label: Redeemed
words.meaning: To redeem or reclaim.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H1350. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: God’s claim on Israel answers fear. The surrounding words stress creation, naming, and belonging.

words.label: Anointed
words.meaning: An anointed person.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H4899. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: Here the text applies the title to Cyrus. The word alone does not identify every anointed figure with the same person.

words.label: Peace
words.meaning: Peace, welfare, or well-being.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H7965. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: A river describes the fullness of peace linked with listening to the commandments.

words.label: Sickness
words.meaning: Sickness or illness.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H2483. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: The speakers reconsider the suffering figure. Translation choices and later interpretation should be distinguished from the dictionary meaning.

words.label: Covenant
words.meaning: A covenant or binding relationship.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H1285. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: The covenant of peace remains even when mountains and hills are pictured as moving.

words.label: Waters
words.meaning: Water.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H4325. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: Water begins an invitation to receive what sustains life without payment.

words.label: Prayer
words.meaning: Prayer.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H8605. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: The house of prayer is described as being for all peoples.

words.label: Fast
words.meaning: A fast, an abstention from food.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H6685. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: The chapter connects the chosen fast with release from oppression and practical care.

words.label: Liberty
words.meaning: Liberty or release.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H1865. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: The proclamation addresses captives within a larger announcement of good news and healing.

words.label: New
words.meaning: New or fresh.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H2319. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: The adjective modifies both heavens and earth in the promise of renewed creation.

words.label: Spirit
words.meaning: Spirit, breath, or wind, depending on context.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H7307. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: Here the phrase describes the humble or contrite condition of a person before God.

words.label: King
words.greekNote: The displayed form occurs in verse 1. Verses 16, 17, and 20 use other forms. Verse 6 uses the related verb βασιλεύσομεν.
words.meaning: A royal ruler. The chapter names rulers of Judah, Syria, Israel, and Assyria.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H4428. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.

words.label: Believe
words.greekNote: This form corresponds to believe. The Greek ends with συνῆτε, meaning understand, where the English has established.
words.meaning: To believe or trust. The Hebrew also uses a form of the same root for being established.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H539. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: The Hebrew connects trust with stability through two forms of the same root.

words.label: Virgin / young woman
words.greekNote: The Greek uses παρθένος, commonly translated virgin.
words.meaning: The Hebrew term refers to a young woman of marriageable age. This English translation uses virgin.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H5959. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: Read the word within the sign given to the house of David. A dictionary entry alone does not settle the identity of the woman or the child.

words.label: Immanuel

words.meaning: The name means God with us.
words.grammar: This is Hebrew word H6005. We show its main form. The form in this verse may look different.
words.discussion: The name is part of the sign announced during the threat against Judah.

guides.title: The Assyrian crisis
guides.description: Follow the Assyrian threat from Lachish to Jerusalem.

steps.title: Locate the two cities
steps.text: Find Lachish on the map. An Assyrian official travels from here to Jerusalem. The line connects the cities; the exact route is unknown.

steps.title: Listen to the argument
steps.text: The speaker challenges trust in Egypt and Hezekiah. How does he use these places to support his argument?

steps.title: A public audience
steps.text: The officials request Aramaic. The speaker addresses the people on the wall in their own language. Why does his choice matter?

steps.title: A threat to move the people
steps.text: Compare the offer of food and land with the promised removal to another land. How does the speech make submission sound attractive?

guides.title: Two accounts, one crisis
guides.description: Compare Isaiah’s account with Assyrian records.

steps.title: The palace viewpoint
steps.text: What does this image emphasize about the victorious king? What does it leave out?

steps.title: The royal inscription
steps.text: Study guide summary: Sennacherib presents Judah’s losses and Hezekiah’s tribute as royal success. The prism does not claim Jerusalem’s capture. Compare this account with Isaiah 37. What does each account emphasize? The photograph shows the Taylor Prism. Luckenbill’s edition translates the separate Chicago Prism.

steps.title: How the account ends
steps.text: Isaiah credits God with saving Jerusalem. Compare this explanation with the Assyrian account. Consider the purpose and limits of each source.

steps.title: Years between events
steps.text: The final verse describes a death many years later. Consecutive verses can describe events that are far apart in time.

guides.title: Babylon and Judah’s future
guides.description: Study the events before and after Isaiah 39.

steps.title: A vulnerable king
steps.text: Chapter 38 describes Hezekiah’s illness and a promise to defend Jerusalem. Chapter order alone does not establish the order of these events.

steps.title: Visitors from Babylon
steps.text: Babylon sends visitors to Hezekiah. Their visit’s exact date is uncertain. The map uses 703 BCE to show the setting.

steps.title: Jerusalem’s later destruction
steps.text: The timeline shows Jerusalem’s destruction in 587/586 BCE. Compare Isaiah’s warning about the palace treasures with this later event. Related authorship study: McClellan compares Isaiah 39’s warning with chapter 40’s perspective after exile. His video explains the term Second Isaiah.

steps.title: Persia takes Babylon
steps.text: The timeline ends with Cyrus’s conquest. The Cyrus Cylinder gives a royal account. It does not mention the return of Judah’s exiles.

guides.title: Worship and justice
guides.description: Trace care for vulnerable people across Isaiah.

steps.title: Learn to do good
steps.text: Read Isaiah 1:10–20. Compare the criticism of worship with the command to defend vulnerable people.

steps.title: The vineyard
steps.text: Read Isaiah 5:1–7. Identify the fruit the vineyard owner expected and what he received.

steps.title: The chosen fast
steps.text: Read Isaiah 58:3–12. Name the actions that make worship visible in daily life.

guides.title: Comfort and return
guides.description: Follow images of strength, remembrance, and renewed belonging.

steps.title: Strength for the weary
steps.text: Read Isaiah 40:27–31. Notice how the reply addresses the complaint that God does not see the people.

steps.title: Zion remembered
steps.text: Read Isaiah 49:14–18. Compare Zion’s complaint with the images in God’s answer.

steps.title: A covenant of peace
steps.text: Read Isaiah 54:7–17. Consider how the promise answers abandonment and fear.

guides.title: Read the servant passages
guides.description: Compare the servant’s work, suffering, and vindication.

steps.title: Justice without crushing
steps.text: Read Isaiah 42:1–9. Describe the servant’s task and manner. Keep questions of identity separate from these observations.

steps.title: A wider mission
steps.text: Read Isaiah 49:1–6. Notice how the passage names Israel and also describes restoring Israel.

steps.title: Suffering and vindication
steps.text: Read Isaiah 52:13 through 53:12. Track the speakers and how their view of the servant changes. Compare Christian interpretation in LDS mode.

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major corridor linked Egypt with the coastal plain and the northern Levant. Trade, diplomacy, and imperial armies used its connected plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed the Carmel region and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later label; This study guide uses the descriptive name international coastal highway.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Strong evidence supports the corridor. The displayed line is approximate, and its branches and exact roadbeds changed over time.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus corridor
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean, the upper Jordan region, and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and inland crossings made this corridor important for regional trade and military travel between the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The main connection is well supported. The line shows a corridor rather than one fixed or continuously built road.

ancientRoads.title: Central ridge road
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south road followed the central highlands from Beersheba through Hebron, Jerusalem, Bethel, Shechem, and toward the Jezreel Valley.
ancientRoads.detail: This route linked the principal highland settlements of Judah and Israel. It avoided some lowland obstacles but still depended on ridges, saddles, and local descents.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The highland corridor is well supported. The precise track could divide or shift between nearby ridges and settlements.

ancientRoads.title: Jordan Valley and Arabah corridor
ancientRoads.summary: A long north–south corridor used the Arabah and Jordan Valley between the Gulf of Aqaba, the Dead Sea region, Jericho, Beth Shean, and Galilee.
ancientRoads.detail: Travelers used several tracks on both sides of the valley. Fords and seasonal conditions affected where people crossed the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The valley corridor is secure, but the displayed line combines several possible tracks and does not mark specific fords.

ancientRoads.title: Shephelah road
ancientRoads.summary: This route ran through Judah’s western lowlands between Beersheba, Lachish, the valleys below Jerusalem, Gezer, and Aphek.
ancientRoads.detail: The Shephelah formed a connected lowland zone between the coastal plain and the Judean hills. Fortified towns near the route guarded approaches into the highlands.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional route is well supported. Local branches between valleys and fortified towns are simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western approach connected the coastal plain and Aijalon Valley with Jerusalem through the Beth-horon ascent.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass and connection are well supported. The line does not claim an exact eighth-century roadbed at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Lachish–Jerusalem approaches
ancientRoads.summary: Routes through the Shephelah valleys connected Lachish and nearby fortified towns with the Judean highlands and Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.detail: Isaiah 36 names travel from Lachish to Jerusalem, but it does not identify the chosen road. This corridor shows one common western approach through the lowlands and hill passes.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is probable. The exact route used in 701 BCE is unknown, so the line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Jerusalem–Jericho road
ancientRoads.summary: This steep east–west route connected Jerusalem with Jericho, the Jordan Valley, and crossings toward Transjordan.
ancientRoads.detail: The road descended rapidly through dry and broken terrain. It gave Jerusalem access to the valley and to routes east of the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection is well supported. The displayed bends are approximate and do not identify one preserved Iron Age roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Transjordan plateau corridor
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south corridor crossed the Transjordan plateau through Edom, Moab, Ammon, Gilead, and toward Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: This connected series of plateau roads is often called the King’s Highway. It supported regional exchange and linked settlements east of the Jordan with Arabia, Syria, and western crossings.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The broad corridor is well known, but it was not one uniformly engineered road. The eighth-century alignment and local branches remain approximate.

ancientRoads.title: Damascus–Hamath–Aleppo corridor
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south inland corridor connected Damascus with the Orontes valley, Hamath, and Aleppo.
ancientRoads.detail: Aleppo stood where routes between Anatolia, inner Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Mediterranean met. This line follows the broad inland connection through the Orontes corridor rather than the desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is well supported, but the evidence does not define one fixed Iron Age track for its full length. The line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Aleppo–Euphrates approach
ancientRoads.summary: This road linked Aleppo with the Euphrates crossing near Til Barsip and the wider Assyrian network.
ancientRoads.detail: Assyrian campaign records and archaeological geography support a route from the Euphrates through the Sajur and Manbij area, then west across the Jabbul plain toward Aleppo.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection and principal approach are well supported. The displayed bends simplify several local valleys and possible parallel tracks.

ancientRoads.title: Assyrian King’s Road to Nineveh
ancientRoads.summary: The Neo-Assyrian state road connected the western provinces with the Assyrian heartland and its capital at Nineveh.
ancientRoads.detail: The documented route crossed the Euphrates at Til Barsip, the Balih south of Harran, and Habur tributaries between Guzana and Nasibina before it reached the Tigris at Nineveh. Royal messengers used relays of mules and road stations.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The named crossings and stations are well supported. The line between them is a regional reconstruction, not a surveyed roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Assyrian Tigris corridor
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route along the Tigris linked Nineveh, Kalhu, and Assur in the Assyrian heartland.
ancientRoads.detail: Kalhu held a central position between Assur and Nineveh. It served long-distance movement on land and on the river and became an Assyrian royal capital.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The cities and the north–south connection are secure. The displayed line is a corridor and does not separate land travel from nearby river transport at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Arbela–Babylonia corridor
ancientRoads.summary: An eastern branch connected Kalhu with Arbela, the western edge of the Zagros Mountains, and routes south into Babylonia.
ancientRoads.detail: Kalhu controlled an eastward route through Arbela. The connection then followed the western Zagros fringe toward Babylonia, avoiding a direct crossing of the central desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is supported, but the precise southern alignment and stations are uncertain. The line is dashed.

chapterStudies.text: I heard the Lord’s voice, saying, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” Then I said, “Here I am. Send me!”

chapterStudies.text: The head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is Remaliah’s son. If you will not believe, surely you shall not be established.’ ”

chapterStudies.text: Of the increase of his government and of peace there shall be no end, on David’s throne, and on his kingdom, to establish it, and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness from that time on, even forever. The zeal of the LORD of Armies will perform this.

chapterStudies.context: The tool cannot claim the skill of the person who uses it. This image exposes Assyria's pride without excusing the empire's violence.
chapterStudies.text: Should an ax brag against him who chops with it? Should a saw exalt itself above him who saws with it? As if a rod should lift those who lift it up, or as if a staff should lift up someone who is not wood.

chapterStudies.context: The ruler's judgment protects poor and humble people. Read the peaceful animals in verses 6–9 as part of this wider vision of a just world.
chapterStudies.text: but he will judge the poor with righteousness, and decide with equity for the humble of the earth. He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth; and with the breath of his lips he will kill the wicked.

chapterStudies.context: Water gives the song a concrete image of received life and joy. Thanksgiving then becomes a public invitation to tell others what God has done.
chapterStudies.text: Therefore with joy you will draw water out of the wells of salvation.

chapterStudies.context: The attack on Babylon belongs within a wider judgment on arrogance and evil. The cosmic images amplify the scale of that judgment.
chapterStudies.text: I will punish the world for their evil, and the wicked for their iniquity. I will cause the arrogance of the proud to cease, and will humble the arrogance of the terrible.

chapterStudies.context: The text introduces the poem as a taunt against Babylon's king. Keep this stated target in view when reading the fallen morning star in verse 12.
chapterStudies.text: that you will take up this parable against the king of Babylon, and say, “How the oppressor has ceased! The golden city has ceased!”

chapterStudies.context: The speaker grieves for Moab while describing its flight. The named roads and towns express human suffering; they do not establish a complete refugee itinerary.
chapterStudies.text: My heart cries out for Moab! Her nobles flee to Zoar, to Eglath Shelishiyah; for they go up by the ascent of Luhith with weeping; for on the way to Horonaim, they raise up a cry of destruction.

chapterStudies.context: The appeal asks for protection from a destroyer. Read it with the call for a just throne in verse 5 and the lament over Moab's pride.
chapterStudies.text: Let my outcasts dwell with you! As for Moab, be a hiding place for him from the face of the destroyer. For the extortionist is brought to nothing. Destruction ceases. The oppressors are consumed out of the land.

chapterStudies.context: Loss changes where people look for security. Verse 8 contrasts the Maker with altars and objects made by human hands.
chapterStudies.text: In that day, people will look to their Maker, and their eyes will have respect for the Holy One of Israel.

chapterStudies.context: The chapter ends with a gift brought to Zion from a distant people. The earlier messengers and the final gift belong to different scenes in the poem.
chapterStudies.text: In that time, a present will be brought to the LORD of Armies from a people tall and smooth, even from a people awesome from their beginning onward, a nation that measures out and treads down, whose land the rivers divide, to the place of the name of the LORD of Armies, Mount Zion.

chapterStudies.context: The blessing applies language of belonging to Egypt and Assyria as well as Israel. This ending changes the direction of a chapter that began with Egypt's distress.
chapterStudies.text: because the LORD of Armies has blessed them, saying, “Blessed be Egypt my people, Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance.”

chapterStudies.context: The sign exposes the weakness of the powers in which people placed their hope. Isaiah's action in verses 2–4 represents captivity, not a travel account.
chapterStudies.text: They will be dismayed and confounded, because of Ethiopia their expectation, and of Egypt their glory.

chapterStudies.context: Food and water answer the needs of people fleeing violence. The scene about Arabia follows the separate announcements concerning Babylon and Dumah.
chapterStudies.text: They brought water to him who was thirsty. The inhabitants of the land of Tema met the fugitives with their bread.

chapterStudies.context: The criticism concerns failure to look to God while preparing defenses. The verse names waterworks but does not identify every surviving structure in Jerusalem.
chapterStudies.text: You also made a reservoir between the two walls for the water of the old pool. But you didn’t look to him who had done this, neither did you have respect for him who planned it long ago.

chapterStudies.context: Tyre's loss becomes a judgment on pride in wealth and status. Its trading connections explain why the lament reaches beyond one city.
chapterStudies.text: The LORD of Armies has planned it, to stain the pride of all glory, to bring into contempt all the honorable of the earth.

chapterStudies.context: The vision links a damaged world with broken obligations. Its wide scope crosses social ranks rather than describing one local campaign.
chapterStudies.text: The earth also is polluted under its inhabitants, because they have transgressed the laws, violated the statutes, and broken the everlasting covenant.

chapterStudies.context: The promise reaches death, grief, and public shame. Read it beside the feast for all peoples in verse 6.
chapterStudies.text: He has swallowed up death forever! The Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces. He will take the reproach of his people away from off all the earth, for the LORD has spoken it.

chapterStudies.context: Hope for the dead follows images of failed childbirth and national distress. The song holds this hope beside the command to wait through judgment.
chapterStudies.text: Your dead shall live. Their dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.

chapterStudies.context: Fruitfulness reverses the failed vineyard in chapter 5. The chapter also describes judgment and a gathering to worship in Jerusalem.
chapterStudies.text: In days to come, Jacob will take root. Israel will blossom and bud. They will fill the surface of the world with fruit.

chapterStudies.context: A secure foundation answers the rulers' false security in verses 14–15. Compare this promise with the warning about failed understanding earlier in the chapter.
chapterStudies.text: Therefore the Lord GOD says, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.

chapterStudies.context: Words of worship do not guarantee a willing heart. This accusation belongs with the images of sealed writing and failed understanding.
chapterStudies.text: The Lord said, “Because this people draws near with their mouth and honors me with their lips, but they have removed their heart far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment of men which has been taught;

chapterStudies.context: The offer of rest stands against the rush to obtain Egyptian help. The verse ends by recording refusal, so the promise also exposes a failed choice.
chapterStudies.text: For thus said the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel, “You will be saved in returning and rest. Your strength will be in quietness and in confidence.” You refused,

chapterStudies.context: The contrast names the limits of human military power. The chapter challenges reliance on Egypt without treating horses or planning as divine protection.
chapterStudies.text: Now the Egyptians are men, and not God; and their horses flesh, and not spirit. When the LORD stretches out his hand, both he who helps shall stumble, and he who is helped shall fall, and they all shall be consumed together.

chapterStudies.context: Peace follows righteousness. Read the quiet homes in verse 18 with the preceding promise that the spirit will bring justice to the land.
chapterStudies.text: The work of righteousness will be peace, and the effect of righteousness, quietness and confidence forever.

chapterStudies.context: Judgment, law, and kingship are joined in the LORD. This confession answers the chapter's broken agreements, danger, and longing for security.
chapterStudies.text: For the LORD is our judge. The LORD is our lawgiver. The LORD is our king. He will save us.

chapterStudies.context: The poem names Zion's cause within its judgment on Edom. Its devastated landscape is poetic judgment imagery, not a dated map of one invasion.
chapterStudies.text: For the LORD has a day of vengeance, a year of recompense for the cause of Zion.

chapterStudies.context: The road ends with redeemed people returning to Zion in joy. The wilderness, healing, and safe passage belong to the same restoration vision.
chapterStudies.text: Then the LORD’s ransomed ones will return, and come with singing to Zion; and everlasting joy will be on their heads. They will obtain gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing will flee away.”

chapterStudies.context: The Assyrian speaker uses a broken reed to attack trust in Egypt. This is part of his argument to Jerusalem, not the narrator's neutral description.
chapterStudies.text: Behold, you trust in the staff of this bruised reed, even in Egypt, which if a man leans on it, it will go into his hand and pierce it. So is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him.

chapterStudies.context: Hezekiah asks for rescue so that other kingdoms will recognize the LORD. Compare this purpose with the self-praise in Assyrian royal records.
chapterStudies.text: Now therefore, LORD our God, save us from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you are the LORD, even you only.”

chapterStudies.context: The speaker connects recovery with renewed life before God. The surrounding song moves through fear, distress, gratitude, and a duty to tell the next generation.
chapterStudies.text: Lord, men live by these things; and my spirit finds life in all of them. You restore me, and cause me to live.

chapterStudies.context: The warning turns attention from displayed wealth to its future removal. The chapter's placement does not by itself establish when the visit occurred.
chapterStudies.text: ‘Behold, the days are coming when all that is in your house, and that which your fathers have stored up until today, will be carried to Babylon. Nothing will be left,’ says the LORD.

chapterStudies.context: The Creator does not share human exhaustion. Verses 29–31 connect that claim with strength for people who feel overlooked and weary.
chapterStudies.text: Haven’t you known? Haven’t you heard? The everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, doesn’t faint. He isn’t weary. His understanding is unsearchable.

chapterStudies.context: The assurance addresses the servant people named as Israel and Jacob in verses 8–9. Later personal applications should retain this collective setting.
chapterStudies.text: Don’t you be afraid, for I am with you. Don’t be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you. Yes, I will help you. Yes, I will uphold you with the right hand of my righteousness.

chapterStudies.context: The servant brings justice without destroying what is already weak. The manner of the mission matters alongside the question of the servant's identity.
chapterStudies.text: He won’t break a bruised reed. He won’t quench a dimly burning wick. He will faithfully bring justice.

chapterStudies.context: Naming expresses belonging after the judgment at the end of chapter 42. The assurances about water and fire continue this promise of presence.
chapterStudies.text: But now the LORD who created you, Jacob, and he who formed you, Israel, says: “Don’t be afraid, for I have redeemed you. I have called you by your name. You are mine.

chapterStudies.context: The text names Cyrus and connects his work with Jerusalem and the temple. A separate Persian royal object can illuminate his policies without proving every claim in this prophecy.
chapterStudies.text: who says of Cyrus, ‘He is my shepherd, and shall perform all my pleasure,’ even saying of Jerusalem, ‘She will be built;’ and of the temple, ‘Your foundation will be laid.’ ”

chapterStudies.context: Cyrus receives a role in God's purpose even though verses 4–5 say he does not know the LORD. Political power is placed within a larger claim about God's rule.
chapterStudies.text: The LORD says to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have held to subdue nations before him and strip kings of their armor, to open the doors before him, and the gates shall not be shut:

chapterStudies.context: God carries the people across their lives. This reverses the opening picture of people and animals carrying idols that cannot save their carriers.
chapterStudies.text: Even to old age I am he, and even to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear. Yes, I will carry, and will deliver.

chapterStudies.context: Babylon's confidence depends on the belief that no one can hold it accountable. The poem removes that security along with the city's royal status.
chapterStudies.text: For you have trusted in your wickedness. You have said, ‘No one sees me.’ Your wisdom and your knowledge has perverted you. You have said in your heart, ‘I am, and there is no one else besides me.’

chapterStudies.context: The command to leave Babylon leads into an announcement of redemption. Verse 21 uses water in the wilderness to connect departure with divine provision.
chapterStudies.text: Leave Babylon! Flee from the Chaldeans! With the sound of joyful shouting announce this, tell it even to the end of the earth; say, “The LORD has redeemed his servant Jacob!”

chapterStudies.context: A mother's care answers Zion's complaint of being forgotten in verse 14. The engraved palms in verse 16 extend the assurance of remembrance.
chapterStudies.text: “Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? Yes, these may forget, yet I will not forget you!

chapterStudies.context: The servant listens before speaking to weary people. The following verses connect this listening with obedience and suffering.
chapterStudies.text: The Lord GOD has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with words him who is weary. He awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.

chapterStudies.context: Restoration changes waste ground into a garden. The chapter asks its listeners to remember earlier acts of God while waiting for comfort.
chapterStudies.text: For the LORD has comforted Zion. He has comforted all her waste places, and has made her wilderness like Eden, and her desert like the garden of the LORD. Joy and gladness will be found in them, thanksgiving, and the voice of melody.

chapterStudies.context: The messenger announces peace, salvation, and God's reign. Verses 8–12 turn this announcement into celebration and a call to leave in purity.
chapterStudies.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news, who proclaims salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”

chapterStudies.context: The speakers revise their judgment of the servant. What they first understood as punishment becomes suffering borne for others.
chapterStudies.text: Surely he has borne our sickness and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted.

chapterStudies.context: The covenant of peace is pictured as more secure than mountains. Read this assurance as an answer to the earlier images of abandonment and shame.
chapterStudies.text: For the mountains may depart, and the hills be removed, but my loving kindness will not depart from you, and my covenant of peace will not be removed,” says the LORD who has mercy on you.

chapterStudies.context: Food and drink are offered to people without money. Verses 2–3 explain the invitation through listening, life, and an enduring covenant.
chapterStudies.text: “Hey! Come, everyone who thirsts, to the waters! Come, he who has no money, buy, and eat! Yes, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.

chapterStudies.context: The promise includes the foreigners and eunuchs addressed in verses 3–6. Worship and belonging are connected with covenant faithfulness rather than ancestry alone.
chapterStudies.text: I will bring these to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer. Their burnt offerings and their sacrifices will be accepted on my altar; for my house will be called a house of prayer for all peoples.”

chapterStudies.context: The high and holy God also dwells with humble, contrite people. The promise of renewal follows the chapter's criticism of false worship.
chapterStudies.text: For the high and lofty One who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy, says: “I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also who is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite.

chapterStudies.context: The chosen fast includes food, shelter, clothing, and care for kin. These duties explain why fasting alongside oppression fails in the earlier verses.
chapterStudies.text: Isn’t it to distribute your bread to the hungry, and that you bring the poor who are cast out to your house? When you see the naked, that you cover him; and that you not hide yourself from your own flesh?

chapterStudies.context: The failure of justice and the absence of an intercessor lead to divine action. The armor in verse 17 develops this image of rescue and judgment.
chapterStudies.text: He saw that there was no man, and wondered that there was no intercessor. Therefore his own arm brought salvation to him; and his righteousness sustained him.

chapterStudies.context: Zion's light draws nations and rulers. The vision concerns the restoration of a humiliated city, not a reconstructed route for a historical procession.
chapterStudies.text: Nations will come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising.

chapterStudies.context: The speaker's anointing serves poor, wounded, and captive people. The following verses join release with comfort and the rebuilding of ruined communities.
chapterStudies.text: The Lord GOD’s Spirit is on me, because the LORD has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives and release to those who are bound,

chapterStudies.context: New names replace abandonment and desolation. The marriage image describes a restored relationship between the land, its people, and God.
chapterStudies.text: You will not be called Forsaken any more, nor will your land be called Desolate any more; but you will be called Hephzibah, and your land Beulah; for the LORD delights in you, and your land will be married.

chapterStudies.context: The prayer recalls mercy and rescue before confessing rebellion and absence. Remembered care gives the speakers grounds to ask for help again.
chapterStudies.text: In all their affliction he was afflicted, and the angel of his presence saved them. In his love and in his pity he redeemed them. He bore them, and carried them all the days of old.

chapterStudies.context: The clay image expresses dependence on the maker. The prayer still names guilt and ruined holy places; trust does not erase that distress.
chapterStudies.text: But now, LORD, you are our Father. We are the clay and you our potter. We all are the work of your hand.

chapterStudies.context: New creation answers the former troubles named in verse 16. The following vision describes joy, homes, fruitful work, and peace.
chapterStudies.text: “For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth; and the former things will not be remembered, nor come into mind.

chapterStudies.context: God values humility and responsiveness to his word. This claim qualifies confidence in a temple that human hands can build.
chapterStudies.text: For my hand has made all these things, and so all these things came to be,” says the LORD: “but I will look to this man, even to he who is poor and of a contrite spirit, and who trembles at my word.
